specStatements.text: The complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas in physics.

These key ideas are of universal application, and we have embedded them throughout the subject content. They underpin many aspects of the science assessment and will therefore be assessed across all papers.
• the use of models, as in the particle model of matter or the wave models of light and of sound
• the concept of cause and effect in explaining such links as those between force and acceleration, or between changes in atomic nuclei and radioactive emissions
• the phenomena of ‘action at a distance’ and the related concept of the field as the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects
• that differences, for example between pressures or temperatures or electrical potentials, are the drivers of change
• that proportionality, for example between weight and mass of an object or between force and extension in a spring, is an important aspect of many models in science
• that physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form.

concepts.definition: One of a small number of ideas that can be used to describe the complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world. A key idea is not a detail belonging to one topic; it is a way of thinking that recurs across the whole subject.

concepts.term: Universal application of the key ideas
concepts.definition: The key ideas apply everywhere in physics. They are embedded throughout the subject content, they underpin many aspects of the science assessment, and they are therefore assessed across all papers rather than in any single topic.

concepts.term: The key ideas listed in the specification
concepts.definition: The key ideas in physics include: the use of models; the concept of cause and effect; ‘action at a distance’ and the related concept of the field; differences as the drivers of change; proportionality; and the expression of physical laws and models in mathematical form.

A simplified representation of a system or process, used to describe it, explain how it behaves and predict what it will do. A model does not have to be a true picture of the thing it represents in order to be useful.

A model in which matter is treated as being made of particles, whose arrangement and movement are used to explain the properties and behaviour of solids, liquids and gases. It is given in the specification as an example of the use of models.

concepts.term: Wave models of light and of sound
concepts.definition: Models in which light and sound are each described as waves, so that quantities such as wavelength, frequency and speed can be used to explain how they travel and how they behave. They are given in the specification as examples of the use of models.

The idea that one physical change brings about another, so that explanations identify which is the cause and which is the effect. Examples given in the specification are the link between force and acceleration, and the link between changes in atomic nuclei and radioactive emissions.

The phenomenon of a force acting between two objects that are not touching. Electrical, magnetic and gravitational forces all act at a distance, unlike contact forces such as friction or normal contact force.

The region around an object in which another object experiences a non-contact force. The concept of the field is the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects: the field is a property of the object producing it and is there whether or not a second object is placed in it.

concepts.term: Differences as the drivers of change
concepts.definition: Change is driven by a difference between two places or two objects, not by a large value at one place on its own. Examples given in the specification are differences between pressures, between temperatures, and between electrical potentials.

Two quantities are directly proportional when one is always the same constant multiple of the other, so that a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin. Proportionality is an important aspect of many models in science: weight is proportional to mass, weight = mass × gravitational field strength, W = m g; and, up to the limit of proportionality, the force on a spring is proportional to its extension, force = spring constant × extension, F = k e.

concepts.term: Physical laws and models in mathematical form
concepts.definition: Physical laws and models are expressed as equations, which state exactly how the quantities are related. Writing a law mathematically allows values to be calculated, predictions to be made and the model to be tested against measurements. Rearranging an equation changes only its form, not the relationship it describes.

misconceptions.question: What is a scientific model?
misconceptions.correct: A model is a simplified representation used to describe, explain and predict behaviour; it may be an idea or an equation, not a physical object.
misconceptions.misconception: A model is a small physical copy of the real thing, like a model aeroplane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language a 'model' is a scaled-down object, and the first models students meet in school are often physical demonstrations.
misconceptions.correction: In physics a model is a way of representing how something behaves. The particle model and the wave models of light and of sound are ideas, not objects, and they earn their place by explaining and predicting behaviour.

misconceptions.question: Does the particle model show what particles really look like?
misconceptions.correct: No. The model represents particles in a simplified way in order to explain behaviour; it is not a picture of what particles actually are.
misconceptions.misconception: Particles really are tiny solid coloured spheres, because that is how the model draws them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams and animations always draw particles as identical spheres, and students take the representation for the reality.
misconceptions.correction: The spheres are a representation chosen because it makes arrangement and movement easy to reason about. The usefulness of the model does not depend on particles looking like that.

misconceptions.question: If a model has a limitation, should it be abandoned?
misconceptions.correct: No. A model with known limitations is still used where it works, provided its limits are understood.
misconceptions.misconception: If a model does not describe everything correctly then it is wrong and should not be used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat scientific statements as simply true or false, so 'not completely accurate' is read as 'false'.
misconceptions.correction: Models are judged by usefulness, not by whether they are complete. A model is used within the range where it explains and predicts well, and a different model is used beyond it.

misconceptions.question: Two quantities change together. Does one cause the other?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Things that happen together may both be caused by something else, or may be unconnected.
misconceptions.misconception: If two things always happen at the same time, one of them must be causing the other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet cause and effect mainly through examples where the link is real, so they treat any association as proof of a cause.
misconceptions.correction: A causal claim needs a mechanism, not just an association. The specification's examples work because there is a physical mechanism: a resultant force acting on a mass produces acceleration, and a change in a nucleus produces an emission.

misconceptions.question: In the link between force and acceleration, which is the cause?
misconceptions.correct: The resultant force is the cause and the acceleration is the effect.
misconceptions.misconception: The object accelerates, and its acceleration is what creates the force on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force and acceleration are always seen together and are related by a single equation, so students reverse the direction of the explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The resultant force acts on the object and the object responds by accelerating: force = mass × acceleration, F = m a. The equation gives the size of the effect, while the force remains the cause.

misconceptions.question: Can a force act between objects that are not touching?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Electrical, magnetic and gravitational forces act at a distance, with no contact between the objects.
misconceptions.misconception: Forces can only act when two objects are touching, so something invisible must be touching in between.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of pushing and pulling is entirely by contact, so a non-contact force feels as though it needs a physical link.
misconceptions.correction: ‘Action at a distance’ is a real phenomenon, and it is analysed using the concept of the field: the object produces a field, and a second object placed in that field experiences a force.

misconceptions.question: When does an object's field exist?
misconceptions.correct: The field is there all the time as a property of the object producing it, whether or not a second object is present.
misconceptions.misconception: A magnetic or gravitational field only appears once a second object is brought close enough to be pulled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The field is only ever detected by its effect on something else, so students conclude that the second object is what creates it.
misconceptions.correction: The second object reveals the field; it does not create it. A magnet has a magnetic field around it even with nothing nearby, just as a planet has a gravitational field.

misconceptions.question: Which object transfers energy to the other by heating?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred by heating from the object at the higher temperature to the object at the lower temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy always moves from the object that stores more energy to the one that stores less.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge the ideas of temperature and stored energy, so the bigger or heavier object is assumed to heat the smaller one.
misconceptions.correction: The driver is the temperature difference, not the amount stored. A small hot block heats a large cool tank, even though the tank's store of energy is far greater.

misconceptions.question: Why does change happen — because a quantity is large, or because there is a difference?
misconceptions.correct: Because there is a difference between two places: in pressure, in temperature or in electrical potential.
misconceptions.misconception: Change happens because a quantity is large at one point — the air is at high pressure, the block is hot, the wire has a voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday phrasing refers to a single value ('high pressure', 'the voltage here'), which hides the fact that two points are always being compared.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing flows when both places are the same, however large the value. Air flows only when the pressures differ, energy is transferred by heating only when the temperatures differ, and charge flows only when there is a potential difference.

misconceptions.question: Does a straight-line graph always show direct proportionality?
misconceptions.correct: No. The line must be straight and must pass through the origin.
misconceptions.misconception: Any straight-line graph shows that the two quantities are directly proportional.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Linear' and 'proportional' are used loosely in conversation, and most straight lines students plot happen to go through the origin.
misconceptions.correction: A straight line that cuts an axis away from the origin shows a constant rate of change but not proportionality, because doubling one quantity does not double the other.

misconceptions.question: If the force on a spring is doubled, what happens to the spring constant?
misconceptions.correct: The spring constant is unchanged; it is a constant for that spring, and the extension doubles instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the force doubles the spring constant, because k is part of the equation and must go up too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat every symbol in an equation as a variable, and do not distinguish the constant of proportionality from the quantities it relates.
misconceptions.correction: In force = spring constant × extension, F = k e, the value of k is fixed for a given spring. That is exactly what makes force and extension directly proportional.

misconceptions.question: What does an equation in physics tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It states how the quantities are related, so it can be used to explain and to predict, not only to calculate.
misconceptions.misconception: The symbols are just shorthand labels, and the equation is only a recipe for getting a number out of a calculator.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equations are most often met in calculation questions, so their role in stating a relationship goes unnoticed.
misconceptions.correction: Physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form. F = m a says that acceleration is proportional to resultant force for a fixed mass — a statement about the world, before any number is substituted.

misconceptions.question: Does rearranging an equation change the physics it describes?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rearranging changes only the form; the relationship between the quantities is identical.
misconceptions.misconception: Writing a = F ÷ m instead of F = m a changes the relationship, so a different rule now applies.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The subject of the equation looks like the thing being 'produced', so moving it appears to move the cause.
misconceptions.correction: F = m a and a = F ÷ m are the same statement. Which form is used depends on which quantity is being calculated; it says nothing about which quantity is the cause.

misconceptions.question: Do ideas from one topic apply in another?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The key ideas are of universal application and are embedded throughout the subject content.
misconceptions.misconception: Each topic has its own separate rules, so an idea learned in electricity has nothing to do with gravity or heating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Teaching, revision guides and exam papers are organised topic by topic, so the connections between topics are easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: The same small number of key ideas runs through every topic. 'Differences drive change', for example, explains fluid flow, heating and electric current alike.

misconceptions.question: Are the key ideas assessed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They underpin many aspects of the science assessment and are assessed across all papers.
misconceptions.misconception: The key ideas are introductory background at the front of the specification and never come up in the exam.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The key ideas are not written as a separate teaching topic with its own recall content, so they look like preamble.
misconceptions.correction: Because they are embedded throughout the subject content, they are assessed through the topics themselves, on every paper rather than in one place.

misconceptions.question: Are weight and mass the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are different quantities, related by weight = mass × gravitational field strength, W = m g.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are the same quantity, just written in different units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday life, and on Earth weight is always the same fixed multiple of mass.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is measured in kilograms and weight is a force measured in newtons. They are directly proportional at a given place, which is why the confusion survives, but they are not the same quantity.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what is meant by a key idea in physics?

options.text: An idea that runs through many topics and describes a wide range of phenomena
options.rationale: The specification states that diverse phenomena can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas.

options.text: A rule that applies only inside the particular topic in which it is first taught
options.rationale: Students who revise topic by topic assume every idea belongs to one topic only.

options.text: A detailed description of one particular phenomenon in great depth
options.rationale: Confuses a key idea with detailed subject content; students equate 'important' with 'detailed'.

options.text: A piece of background reading that is never examined on any paper
options.rationale: Because the key ideas are not a taught topic, students dismiss them as preamble.

mcqs.stem: Energy is transferred from a hot drink to a cooler room, and charge flows through a lamp connected to a cell. Which key idea links these two examples?

options.text: A large store always empties into a store that is smaller
options.rationale: Students substitute amount stored for the difference that actually drives transfer.

options.text: Both are examples of action at a distance through a field
options.rationale: Fields are the most memorable key idea, so students reach for it first.

options.text: The two examples come from separate topics and are unrelated
options.rationale: Topic-by-topic revision makes cross-topic links invisible to students.

options.text: A difference between two places is what drives the change
options.rationale: A temperature difference drives the heating and a potential difference drives the charge flow.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is listed in the specification as a key idea in physics?

options.text: That each separate area of physics is governed by its own set of rules
options.rationale: Matches how students experience the course, so it sounds authoritative.

options.text: That differences, such as those between temperatures, drive change
options.rationale: This is one of the key ideas listed in the specification.

options.text: That background ideas are read about but are never actually assessed
options.rationale: Students expect anything not taught as a topic to be non-examinable.

options.text: That every graph plotted in physics turns out to be a straight line
options.rationale: Overgeneralises from the many proportional relationships met early on.

mcqs.stem: How do the key ideas relate to the assessment of GCSE Physics?

options.text: They are background information and are never assessed in the exam
options.rationale: The key ideas have no recall content of their own, so they look unexaminable.

options.text: Each key idea is assessed only within the topic that it belongs to
options.rationale: Assumes ideas are owned by topics rather than being universal.

options.text: They are assessed only on the Higher tier papers of the whole course
options.rationale: Students associate anything abstract with Higher tier demand.

options.text: They are embedded in the content and assessed across all papers
options.rationale: The specification states they underpin the assessment and are assessed across all papers.

mcqs.stem: Why do scientists use a model such as the particle model of matter?

options.text: It is a scaled-down physical copy of the material being studied
options.rationale: Takes the everyday meaning of 'model' as a miniature object.

options.text: It gives a simplified description that explains and predicts behaviour
options.rationale: A model is a simplification whose value lies in explanation and prediction.

options.text: It shows precisely what the particles themselves really look like
options.rationale: Standard diagrams are read as photographs of reality.

options.text: It removes every limitation from the explanation being given
options.rationale: Students believe a model must be complete to be acceptable.

mcqs.stem: A model of matter treats particles as tiny solid spheres, although real particles are not solid spheres. What does this tell you about the model?

options.text: It is wrong, and so it should no longer be used in physics
options.rationale: Treats any inaccuracy as fatal to a model.

options.text: It can still be useful even though it is not a true picture
options.rationale: Models are judged by how well they explain and predict, not by literal accuracy.

options.text: It must be a physical copy of the material it represents
options.rationale: Everyday use of 'model' as a scale object drives this choice.

options.text: Particles really are solid spheres, as the model shows them
options.rationale: Students who confuse representation with reality reject the premise.

mcqs.stem: The specification gives 'the wave models of light and of sound' as an example of which key idea?

options.text: The idea that forces act only through direct contact
options.rationale: Students who think waves must be carried by touching particles pick this.

options.text: The idea that all relationships in physics are linear
options.rationale: Wave equations are multiplicative, so 'linear' feels familiar and safe.

options.text: The idea that differences between places drive change
options.rationale: A genuine key idea, chosen by students who match any listed idea to any example.

options.text: The use of models to describe and explain phenomena
options.rationale: The wave models are listed alongside the particle model as examples of modelling.

mcqs.stem: A resultant force acts on an object and the object accelerates. Which statement describes the cause and the effect correctly?

options.text: The acceleration is the cause; the resultant force is the effect
options.rationale: Reverses the causal direction because the two always appear together.

options.text: Neither causes the other; they simply occur at the same moment
options.rationale: Students who distrust causal claims retreat to mere association.

options.text: The resultant force is the cause; the acceleration is the effect
options.rationale: The force acts on the object and the object responds by accelerating.

options.text: The force is an effect of the object's mass being very large
options.rationale: Misreads F = m a as making mass the cause of the force.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus of an unstable atom changes and a radioactive emission is detected. Which statement applies the key idea of cause and effect?

options.text: The change in the nucleus causes the emission that is detected
options.rationale: The specification cites changes in atomic nuclei as the cause of radioactive emissions.

options.text: The emission being detected is what makes the nucleus change
options.rationale: Reverses cause and effect, as with force and acceleration.

options.text: The two events are linked only because they occur together
options.rationale: Treats a genuine mechanism as no more than an association.

options.text: The nucleus emits because a detector is placed close to it
options.rationale: Confuses detecting an emission with causing it.

mcqs.stem: A magnet attracts a steel paperclip without touching it. Which key idea does this illustrate?

options.text: Contact forces, because the air must touch the paperclip
options.rationale: Students insist on a physical link and nominate the air.

options.text: Fields, but only once the paperclip is brought up close
options.rationale: Assumes the second object creates the field it reveals.

options.text: Action at a distance, explained using the idea of a field
options.rationale: A non-contact force between separated objects is analysed using the field concept.

options.text: Proportionality, because the pull grows as distance falls
options.rationale: Any relationship between two quantities gets labelled proportional.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what is meant by a field in physics?

options.text: A region that forms only once a second object is placed close by
options.rationale: The field is only ever detected via a second object, so it seems to need one.

options.text: The surface where two objects make contact and push one another apart
options.rationale: Forces are assumed to require touching, so the field is placed at a contact.

options.text: The path along which a force travels from one object to another
options.rationale: Treats force as a substance in transit rather than an interaction.

options.text: A region in which an object experiences a non-contact force
options.rationale: This is the field concept used to analyse electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects.

mcqs.stem: A small hot metal block is placed in a large tank of cooler water. What determines the direction of the energy transfer by heating?

options.text: Which of the two objects stores the greater amount of energy
options.rationale: Temperature and stored energy are merged, so the tank seems to win.

options.text: How hot the block is, whatever the water's temperature may be
options.rationale: Focuses on one large value instead of the comparison between two.

options.text: The difference in temperature between the block and the water
options.rationale: A temperature difference is the driver of energy transfer by heating.

options.text: The difference in mass between the block and the water in it
options.rationale: Picks the right word 'difference' but attaches it to the wrong quantity.

mcqs.stem: Air rushes out of an inflated balloon when its neck is opened. What drives this flow?

options.text: The high pressure of the air inside the balloon, on its own
options.rationale: Names a single large value rather than a difference between two places.

options.text: The greater quantity of air that is stored inside the balloon
options.rationale: Substitutes amount stored for the difference that drives the flow.

options.text: The difference in pressure between the inside and the outside
options.rationale: The specification gives differences between pressures as a driver of change.

options.text: The temperature of the air inside being higher than outside
options.rationale: Recalls that temperature differences drive change and applies the wrong one.

mcqs.stem: A graph of weight against mass for several objects is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: Gravitational field strength rises as the mass increases
options.rationale: Treats the constant of proportionality as a variable.

options.text: Weight is directly proportional to the mass of the object
options.rationale: A straight line through the origin is exactly the condition for direct proportionality.

options.text: Weight and mass are the same quantity in different units
options.rationale: A proportional graph is read as showing the quantities are identical.

options.text: Weight increases with mass but not in a fixed ratio
options.rationale: Recognises the trend but misses what the origin intercept establishes.

mcqs.stem: What must a graph show if two quantities are to be directly proportional?

options.text: A straight line that passes through the origin
options.rationale: Both conditions are required for direct proportionality.

options.text: A straight line, wherever it happens to cross an axis
options.rationale: 'Linear' and 'proportional' are used interchangeably by students.

options.text: A line whose gradient increases steadily as it rises
options.rationale: Assumes the constant grows as the quantities grow.

options.text: A smooth curve rising steadily from left to right
options.rationale: Associates 'related quantities' with any rising curve.

mcqs.stem: A spring extends 40 mm when a force of 8.0 N is applied. Force and extension remain directly proportional. What is the extension when the force is 12 N?

options.text: 60 mm
options.rationale: The force is multiplied by 1.5, so the extension is 40 mm × 1.5 = 60 mm, with k unchanged.

options.text: 27 mm
options.rationale: Inverts the ratio, calculating 40 × 8 ÷ 12 as if extension fell when force rose.

options.text: 44 mm
options.rationale: Adds the extra 4 N as 4 mm, treating the link as additive rather than proportional.

options.text: 48 mm
options.rationale: Adds the numerical value of the force to the extension, ignoring the units.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that a physical law is expressed in mathematical form?

options.text: The symbols are shorthand labels and carry no relationship
options.rationale: Equations met only in calculations look like recipes, not statements.

options.text: The equation works only in the exact order it is written
options.rationale: The written form is taken to be part of the physics.

options.text: The relationship between the quantities is written as an equation
options.rationale: An equation states exactly how the quantities in the law are related.

options.text: The law is usable only when every value is already known
options.rationale: Overlooks that an equation can be rearranged to find an unknown.

mcqs.stem: The equation F = m a is rearranged to a = F ÷ m. What effect does this rearrangement have?

options.text: It changes the relationship so acceleration now causes force
options.rationale: The subject of the equation is read as the cause of everything else.

options.text: None; it states the same relationship in a different form
options.rationale: Rearranging changes the form of an equation, not the relationship it expresses.

options.text: It makes the symbols stand for different physical quantities
options.rationale: Symbols are treated as labels attached to positions in the equation.

options.text: It shows that acceleration must be measured before force
options.rationale: Confuses the order of calculation with the order of causation.
